passages.happening:
‘Then Bildad the Shuhite replied’ (verse 1). “How long will you go on saying such things? The words of your mouth are a blustering wind” (verse 2).

“Does God pervert justice? Does the Almighty pervert what is right?” (verse 3). Then he says it outright: “When your children sinned against Him, He gave them over to their rebellion” (verse 4).

But if Job will seek God and plead for mercy, “if you are pure and upright, even now He will rouse Himself on your behalf and restore your righteous estate” (verse 6). His small beginnings will grow into a great future.
passages.hearers:
Bildad is the second friend. The name Shuhite may connect him with Shuah, a son of Abraham by Keturah whose descendants were sent to the east (Genesis 25:1-6), though the link is not certain. Like the others he is one of the peoples east of Israel, a man who knows and speaks of God without being an Israelite.

His argument is simpler and harsher than Eliphaz's, and it brings into the open what all three friends believe. Stated in the form he would sign: God is just and never twists what is right; so what happens to people answers to what they have done; so Job should plead with God, and if he is pure, God will restore him.

Bildad is right that God does not pervert justice. The whole Bible says so. His error is to read every event as an immediate verdict, so that suffering proves guilt. Mishpat, justice, is his word in verse 3, and Job will soon take up the same word to ask for his own day in court.
passages.later: The prophets said plainly that the guilt of one is not laid on another: ‘A son will not bear the iniquity of his father, and a father will not bear the iniquity of his son’ (Ezekiel 18:20).
passages.hard:
Did Job's children die because of their sins, as Bildad says?

Bildad says it in verse 4. It is one of the cruelest lines in the book, spoken to a grieving father. The reader knows from chapter 1 that the children's deaths came in the test of Job in heaven, not as punishment for anything they did. Job had even offered sacrifices in case they had sinned in their hearts (1:5). Bildad's claim is a deduction from his theory, not something he knows.

At the end God says that the friends have not spoken rightly about him (42:7). Readers should be careful not to treat Bildad's words as the Bible's teaching just because they stand in the Bible. The book records the friends' speeches in order to test them. No one may tell a grieving parent that their child died for their sins, or for the child's own.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Bildad defended God's justice by accusing the dead. Ask whether you have ever protected your picture of God at someone else's expense. And ask what you would want said to you, if it were your child.

passages.t: The wisdom of the fathers, and a spider's web
passages.happening:
“Please inquire of past generations and consider the discoveries of their fathers. For we were born yesterday and know nothing; our days on earth are but a shadow” (verses 8-9).

Bildad draws a lesson from the marsh. “Does papyrus grow where there is no marsh? Do reeds flourish without water?” (verse 11). Cut off, they wither faster than grass. ‘Such is the destiny of all who forget God; so the hope of the godless will perish’ (verse 13). The godless man trusts a spider's web, and it gives way. He is like a well-watered plant whose roots wrap round the stones, but when he is uprooted, his place says, “I never saw you” (verse 18).

“Behold, God does not reject the blameless, nor will He strengthen the hand of evildoers. He will yet fill your mouth with laughter, and your lips with a shout of joy” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
Bildad's authority is tradition. In the ancient world, wisdom was handed down from fathers and elders and tested over many lifetimes. When he says that all of them were born yesterday, he means that no one life is long enough to overturn what the ancestors learned.

His pictures come from the riverbank and the garden. Papyrus and reeds grew thick in the marshes of the Nile and in wet ground elsewhere, and they withered fast without water. A spider's web looks like shelter but gives way under weight.

The closing promise sounds kind. But notice the word blameless, tam, in verse 20. It is the word the narrator and God have already used of Job (1:1; 1:8). The reader knows that God has not rejected Job. Bildad does not.

Bildad's trust in tradition shows both the strength and the limit of inherited wisdom. Proverbs states patterns about how life usually goes. Job shows what happens when those patterns are made into rules without exceptions.
passages.later: A psalm uses Bildad's picture of a life as a shadow: “Man is like a breath; his days are like a passing shadow” (Psalm 144:4).
passages.asks: Bildad trusted the wisdom of the past more than the man in front of him. Ask what you have been taught about suffering that you have never tested against a real person's story. And ask whether your comfort sounds like a promise or like a warning.
